EXTRA CLASS · KIDS GAMES

Every game, with its rules on the card.

The afternoon-saver class: twenty-six classic games walk the whole day in tour order — throwing and aiming, running and freezing, table games and turns, quiet find-and-solve games, acting and guessing, and the sidewalk classics — and every tile below opens its own simple how-to-play guide a kid can follow.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every game a childhood needs — with the rules on the card.

The Kids Games class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Kitchen Helper and the Doctor Visit: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for the afternoons when somebody says I don’t know what to play. Twenty-six classic games — balloon keep-up, hide and seek, tic-tac-toe, treasure hunt — each one on its own card, and each card opens a simple guide a kid can follow: what you need, how to play, step by step, and one way to make it fresh tomorrow.

The games run in tour order on purpose. The throwing and rolling games come first, because aiming is where little arms start; then the running-and-freezing games that empty a room of wiggles; then the table games that teach waiting a turn; the quiet find-and-solve games for the rainy shelf; the acting games for loud imaginations; and the last group belongs outside — chalk, pavement and a rope on a swing.

THE GAMES, SIX WAYS TO PLAY

Twenty-six cards, six kinds of play.

Twenty-six games in six groups, in the order a real game afternoon unfolds. Tap any picture and it opens its own how-to-play guide — the original card on the left, and the simple kid-followable steps on the right.

THE CLASS GAME

Game Day: let the stack decide.

Stack the cards face down. Draw the top one, read its guide together, play the game — and the winner of each game draws the next card. That is Game Day, and it runs itself: the stack decides everything, the winning gets a crown (and the drawing job), and the afternoon ends only when the stack ends. Losing practice is built right in: short rounds, loud good-games, immediate rematches.

SAME GAME, TWO NAMES

Tic-tac-toe and noughts and crosses. Both are right.

Games travel lighter than words do — the same game grows a new name on every shore, and this class says so out loud. Tic-tac-toe is noughts and crosses in the UK; the jump rope is a skipping rope; the paper plane flies as a paper aeroplane; freeze dance is musical statues across the ocean; the balloon game rides the UK playground word keepy-uppy; and the disc-dropping grid most homes call Connect Four is simply four in a row here — the generic name, playable with buttons on a drawn grid. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that games, like words, come in kinds.

Balloon Keep-Up — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches balloon keep-up in five steps — the game where one rule does all the work.

What is this?

Balloon keep-up is a tapping game: one balloon, everyone playing, and the balloon may never touch the floor.

What does it mean?

Keeping something afloat takes watching, waiting and gentle taps at the right moment — timing, learned with the softest object in the house.

What does the child need to know?

You need one blown-up balloon and a little clear space. Everyone who can reach the balloon can play — no teams, no turns, just keep it up.

Why this matters

A balloon falls slowly, so young players can watch it coming and choose their tap. It is the gentlest catching-and-hitting game ever invented.

What it teaches

Hand-eye timing, gentle-touch control (hard taps send balloons sideways), and quick feet that get the body where the balloon is going.

Words to learn

balloontapupfloatfloorgentlyagain

Say this to your child

“"The balloon is sleepy — tap it up! Gently, gently... it floats! Catch it with a tap before it touches the floor!"”

Step by step

  1. Blow up the balloon and let it float down between you.
  2. Say the rule: "the balloon may never touch the floor."
  3. Tap it up with an open hand — not a slap, a lift.
  4. Chase it wherever it drifts and tap it up again.
  5. Count the saves together — every tap is one point for the whole family.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, two open hands reach up toward one pink balloon — the hands are open because a flat, gentle tap is the whole secret of the game.

Ask your child

"How many taps did we do?" "What happens if we tap too hard?" "Can you save it with your head?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might shout "mine, mine!" and run the balloon down the hallway, count every tap out loud, or invent a rule where the balloon touching a grown-up is double points.

Out in the real world

Every party, every birthday, every picnic with a balloon becomes this game in about nine seconds — now your child knows how to run it.

Try it together

Harder ways: one hand behind your back, everyone sitting cross-legged (the balloon may only fly as high as your head), or two balloons at once for the championship round.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the one rule?" (the balloon never touches the floor) "Do we slap it or tap it?" (tap it gently)

This lesson pairs with the Balloon Keep-Up flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Beanbag Toss — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches beanbag toss — the aiming game where missing is always safe and scoring is always loud.

What is this?

Beanbag toss is a throwing game: stand back from a board with holes and toss the beanbag into one.

What does it mean?

Aiming teaches the eyes and the arm to agree — look at the target, choose the throw, and learn from every short one.

What does the child need to know?

You need a beanbag and something to aim at: a real toss board, a laundry basket, or three bowls on the floor worth 1, 2 and 3 points.

Why this matters

A beanbag lands where it lands and stays — no chasing, no bouncing away — so a whole round of throwing happens in one small room.

What it teaches

Underarm throwing form, target watching, and honest scoring practice when the holes carry numbers.

Words to learn

beanbagtossaimholethrowstepscore

Say this to your child

“"Hold it flat. Look at the hole. Throw it soft and high — under the ceiling, into the target!"”

Step by step

  1. Hold the beanbag flat in your palm like a little pancake.
  2. Look at the hole you want — really look at it.
  3. Swing your arm under, forward and open your fingers.
  4. Walk to your beanbag and pick it up — every throw gets a walk.
  5. Scored? Step back one heel-toe step. Missed twice? Step closer. The game bends to the thrower.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the beanbag flies toward a smiling board whose three holes are numbered 1, 2 and 3 — the numbers make every landing a small score to add up.

Ask your child

"Which hole is worth the most?" "Was your throw too short or too long?" "Can you land one in from one step further back?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might line up three beanbags and fire them one after another, narrate each throw like a sports announcer, or move the target closer and call it "the easy way".

Out in the real world

Beanbag games wait at every fair, every school sports day and every cousin’s backyard — the throw your child practices tonight is the one that wins the prize tomorrow.

Try it together

Tournament rules: five throws each, highest total wins, and the winner sets the next distance. No beanbag? A rolled-up sock is a beanbag that every family already owns.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we hold a beanbag?" (flat in the palm) "What do we do if we miss twice?" (step closer)

This lesson pairs with the Beanbag Toss flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bowling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hallway bowling — the rolling game where the counting after each roll is half the fun.

What is this?

Bowling is a rolling game: send the ball along the floor to knock over the pins standing at the other end.

What does it mean?

Rolling teaches the arm to push straight and low, and the counting between turns turns a game into a math lesson wearing bowling shoes.

What does the child need to know?

You need a soft ball and pins — real ones, or cups, or empty plastic bottles with a little rice inside so they stand up.

Why this matters

Rolling comes earlier than throwing for most children, and bowling gives the roll a job: the pins are waiting to be knocked, and they make a wonderful sound doing it.

What it teaches

Straight-line rolling, counting fallen pins, and the full game loop of knock-down, count and set-up-again.

Words to learn

bowlrollpinsknockcountset upagain

Say this to your child

“"Roll it low and slow — rrrroll! Look at the pins go down! How many fell? One, two, three! Now we set them up for the next bowler."”

Step by step

  1. Set the pins up in a triangle together — point them at the thrower.
  2. Stand back — three big steps is a fair first distance.
  3. Swing the ball between your legs or push it with both hands.
  4. Roll it LOW — a ball that flies is a ball that misses.
  5. Count the fallen pins out loud, then set them up for the next bowler.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the pink ball rolls up the lane toward ten white pins standing in their triangle — the triangle shape is how real pins stand, so every ball can knock more than one.

Ask your child

"How many pins fell?" "Which is louder — a strike or a gutter ball?" "Can you roll it slow enough that the last pin falls last?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might invent strike dances, roll one pin at a time on purpose to make the game last, or insist on setting the pins up alone — the engineer of the alley.

Out in the real world

Bowling alleys rent small balls and light pins for exactly this game — the hallway version is the try-out, and the real lanes are the graduation.

Try it together

Fair turns: one roll each, two rolls if you are feeling generous, and the set-up job travels with the turn. Three bottles is a hallway alley; ten is a championship.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does the ball roll high or low?" (low) "What do we do after we knock the pins?" (count them, then set them up)

This lesson pairs with the Bowling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hoop Toss — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hoop toss — the ring game where every peg is worth a different number of points.

What is this?

Hoop toss is a throwing game: toss the rings so they land around the pegs, and the peg you ring decides your points.

What does it mean?

Choosing your target is the real lesson — the near peg is easy for 10, the far peg is hard for 50, and every turn is a small brave decision.

What does the child need to know?

You need rings (or jar lids, or paper plates with the middle cut out) and pegs or bottles to ring — near ones and far ones.

Why this matters

Scoring gives the game a story: tallies on paper, totals to add, a champion to crown — the math rides inside the game.

What it teaches

Flat-ring throwing, target choice, tally marking, and adding round numbers by tens.

Words to learn

hoopringtosspegpointstallychampion

Say this to your child

“"Hold the ring flat. Choose your peg — the near one is easy, the far one is fifty! Let it fly flat... does it ring?"”

Step by step

  1. Set the pegs out — one close, one far, and one in the middle.
  2. Say the worth: near peg 10, middle 20, far 50 (the card’s rings count by tens).
  3. Hold the ring flat, like a frisbee, elbow relaxed.
  4. Toss it flat and gentle — a spinning ring lands ringed.
  5. Tally your points on paper — one mark per ten — and add them up after five rounds.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the stand shows four scoring rings — 10, 20, 30 and 50 — with three hoops lying on the ground waiting for their turn to fly.

Ask your child

"Which peg will you aim for, and why?" "How many tens is 30?" "What is your plan for the fifty?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might go safe-and-steady on the ten peg every round, or spend all five throws chasing the fifty — both are honest strategies, and the tallies will tell the story.

Out in the real world

Ring toss stands appear at every fair and every school fête with the same rule — and the tally-adding you practice here is the same math the ticket booth does.

Try it together

Champion rules: five rings each, add the tallies, crown the champion, immediate rematch. Backwards round: the far peg is worth 10 and the near one is worth 50 — everything flips.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we hold the ring?" (flat, like a frisbee) "Which peg is worth the most?" (the far one — fifty)

This lesson pairs with the Hoop Toss flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Paper Plane Target — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches paper plane target — a folding game and a flying game joined at the crease.

What is this?

Paper plane target is an aiming game: fold a plane, then fly it at a target on the floor — a drawn bullseye, a hoop, or a laundry basket.

What does it mean?

A plane is a throw that keeps going after your hand lets go — the folds decide the flight, and every flight teaches the next fold.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper (one sheet per plane), and a target: a paper-plate bullseye on the floor, a hoop, or the basket that lost its socks.

Why this matters

The folding is real craft with a job at the end, and the target gives every flight a story — close miss, bullseye, or the legendary basket landing.

What it teaches

Paper folding (the fine-motor art of exact creases), underarm flight throws, and distance-plus-accuracy aiming.

Words to learn

paperplanefoldcreasethrowflytarget

Say this to your child

“"Fold the corners to the middle — crease it flat! Now stand behind the line, aim the nose at the bullseye, and glide it — smooth and gentle."”

Step by step

  1. Fold the plane: paper in half the long way, open it, fold the two top corners to the middle line, fold the new point down, fold the sides to the middle once more.
  2. Draw a bullseye on paper or put a basket where the floor is clear.
  3. Stand behind the line — three big steps from the target.
  4. Hold the plane under its belly, aim, and let it glide — a smooth push, not a hard slam.
  5. Score it: one point for a close landing, three for the bullseye, five for the basket.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, two paper planes fly toward a red-and-white target on a stand — one plane is close and one is still climbing, because every flight lands somewhere different.

Ask your child

"Which fold made the biggest difference?" "What happens when you throw harder?" "Where should the nose point at the moment you let go?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might name every plane before its first flight, fold a fleet of five and fly them in formation, or adjust the wing tips after every throw like a real test pilot.

Out in the real world

In the UK the same plane is a paper aeroplane — same folds, same flight. Folding planes is a game that travels: one sheet of paper turns any waiting room into a target range.

Try it together

Best of five flights each. Then the engineering round: bend the back edges of the wings up a little, fly again, and see what changed — real aerodynamics, discovered by hand.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we fold first?" (the paper in half, the long way) "Do we slam the plane or glide it?" (glide it — smooth and gentle)

This lesson pairs with the Paper Plane Target flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Duck, Duck, Goose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches duck, duck, goose — the circle game that every party and every playground already knows.

What is this?

Duck, duck, goose is a circle game: one player walks around tapping heads saying "duck" — until they pick a goose, and the chase is on.

What does it mean?

The game teaches the wait-and-go switch: sitting players hold still, and the goose must burst into running at one exact word.

What does the child need to know?

You need three or more players and floor space for a circle. No equipment at all — the circle and the words are the whole game.

Why this matters

It is the fairest running game for mixed ages: the tapper walks, the goose runs, and every child gets both jobs in one round.

What it teaches

Turn-taking, impulse control (waiting while heads get tapped), sprinting, and the social art of choosing a goose kindly.

Words to learn

circleduckgoosetaprunchasespot

Say this to your child

“"Duck... duck... duck... GOOSE! Run, run, run around the ring! Reach the spot and sit down before the goose catches you!"”

Step by step

  1. Everyone sits cross-legged in a circle, knees almost touching.
  2. One player is the tapper — everyone else is a sitting duck.
  3. The tapper walks around the outside, tapping each head: "duck... duck... duck..."
  4. On one head the tapper says "GOOSE!" — and the goose leaps up and chases them around the circle.
  5. The tapper runs for the goose’s empty spot; if they sit first, the goose is the new tapper. If the goose catches them, the goose sits and the tapper goes again.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the children sit in a ring with their knees together while one child runs around the outside — the dotted line shows the tapper’s path around the circle.

Ask your child

"What does the tapper say on every head?" (duck) "What happens when they say goose?" (the goose chases) "Where does the tapper run?" (to the goose’s empty spot)

What your child can say or do

Your child might stretch "duuuuck" for ten heads to build the suspense, pick their best friend as the goose every time, or run so hard around the ring that sitting down takes three tries.

Out in the real world

Birthday parties, family reunions, playgrounds at recess — duck, duck, goose is the game children run themselves, and now yours knows the whole script.

Try it together

Kind rules: the tapper walks, the goose runs, nobody catches anyone for the first three rounds. Goose-picker’s honor: everyone gets picked within three rounds — the choosing is a kindness job.

Understanding check

Ask: "What word starts the chase?" (goose) "What do we do when we are sitting?" (hold still and wait)

This lesson pairs with the Duck, Duck, Goose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Follow the Leader — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches follow the leader — the copying game where the leader invents the world and everyone walks in it.

What is this?

Follow the leader is a moving game: one player leads and does any move at all, and everyone behind copies it exactly.

What does it mean?

Copying a moving body is watching, understanding and matching at the same time — and leading is deciding, which is its own quiet confidence lesson.

What does the child need to know?

You need two or more players and a little room to move — a hallway, a yard, a circle of carpet. No equipment, no counting, no winner.

Why this matters

The game has no losing and no sitting out — the shyest player can lead with the smallest moves and the loudest one can lead with cartwheels.

What it teaches

Body copying (mirror skills in motion), watching closely, waiting for the next move, and the courage to be the one in front.

Words to learn

leaderfollowcopymarchhoptiptoenext

Say this to your child

“"Follow the leader — do what I do! March, march — now hop! Now tiptoe like a mouse... shh! New leader — you decide the moves!"”

Step by step

  1. Line up behind the leader — one arm’s length apart.
  2. The leader moves and everyone copies: march, hop, tiptoe, spin, wave.
  3. New move? The whole line switches instantly — the leader owns the moves.
  4. Every minute or so, the leader says "new leader!" and hands the crown to the player behind them.
  5. Everyone gets the crown at least once — the game ends when everybody has led.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the first child marches and points the way while the second child copies — the leader’s arm is up because the moves travel down the line.

Ask your child

"What did the leader do first?" "Which move was the hardest to copy?" "What move will you invent when you are the leader?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might invent a move chain — jump, spin, freeze — and repeat it like a dance, or lead the line on a full tour of the house, narrating like a tour guide.

Out in the real world

Any walk anywhere becomes this game: follow the leader down the sidewalk, through the store, to the car. The copying muscles are the same ones dance class and sports practice use.

Try it together

Silly rounds: the leader may only move like animals. Quiet rounds: tiptoe and whisper moves only. Backwards round: the line leads and the leader copies — chaos, crowned.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the follower do?" (copy every move) "When does the crown move?" (when the leader says "new leader")

This lesson pairs with the Follow the Leader flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Freeze Dance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches freeze dance — the dancing game with one giant stop button, known across the ocean as musical statues.

What is this?

Freeze dance is a music game: while the music plays, everyone dances; when it stops, everyone freezes — and nobody may move a muscle.

What does it mean?

Stopping your own body on a signal is a real self-control skill — this is the only game where practicing it feels like a party.

What does the child need to know?

You need music (a phone speaker is fine) and floor space. Two or more players — and a DJ who stops the music at the silliest possible moments.

Why this matters

Every child already knows how to dance; this game adds the part they love almost as much — the freeze, held with a wobbling grin.

What it teaches

Listening, starting and stopping on a signal, body control in stillness, and the comedy of held poses.

Words to learn

musicdancefreezestopstatuestillagain

Say this to your child

“"When the music plays — dance, dance, dance! When it stops — FREEZE! Hold it... hold it... hold it... and — dance again!"”

Step by step

  1. Start the music and dance — big moves, silly moves, any moves.
  2. The DJ stops the music without warning.
  3. Everybody FREEZES — like a statue, like a robot, like a snowman.
  4. Anyone who wiggles after the freeze does one funny job (hop three times) and rejoins — nobody really sits out.
  5. Play again and again — the DJ’s whole art is the surprise.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the child dances mid-move with one music note floating beside them — the note means the music is ON, and the frozen leg says the stop could come at any moment.

Ask your child

"What do we do when the music stops?" (freeze like a statue) "What was your best frozen pose?" "Can you freeze in the middle of a jump?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might hold a freeze so hard they fall over politely, invent statue themes (superheroes, animals, sleepy statues), or beg to be the DJ by round three.

Out in the real world

American families say freeze dance; British families say musical statues — two names, one game, and it appears at every party on both shores.

Try it together

Theme rounds: freeze as animals, freeze as superheroes, freeze in the shape of a letter. Slow-music round: dance in slow motion so the freeze is barely a change at all — the hardest freeze there is.

Understanding check

Ask: "When do we dance?" (while the music plays) "When do we freeze?" (the moment it stops) "What is the DJ’s job?" (stop the music at a surprise moment)

This lesson pairs with the Freeze Dance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hide and Seek — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hide and seek — the oldest game in the world, played in every house with more than one room.

What is this?

Hide and seek is a seeking game: the seeker counts to ten out loud while everyone hides, then finds them one by one.

What does it mean?

Hiding teaches quiet and stillness; seeking teaches memory — where WERE they last time? — and both jobs are real brain work.

What does the child need to know?

You need two or more players and agreed hiding zones: hiders stay where a grown-up can find them in one look, and no hiding where doors close.

Why this matters

The counting is loud, the hiding is silent, and the finding ends in giggles — hide and seek is the whole emotional range of childhood in one game.

What it teaches

Counting out loud (the game’s built-in math), quiet-body hiding, memory for places, and the patience of the seeker.

Words to learn

hideseekcountreadyfoundspotagain

Say this to your child

“"One... two... three... (louder) ...nine, TEN! Ready or not, here I come! I wonder where everybody is hiding..."”

Step by step

  1. Agree the rules before round one: which rooms are in play, and no hiding where doors close.
  2. The seeker closes their eyes and counts out loud to ten — loud, so the hiders can hear.
  3. Everybody hides fast while the counting runs.
  4. "Ready or not, here I come!" — the seeker finds each hider, one by one, kindly.
  5. The first one found is the next seeker — or the last one found, if your family plays it that way. Agree it before you start.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one child covers their eyes to count while another peeks from behind a bush — the counting hands and the peeking eyes are the two halves of the game.

Ask your child

"What does the seeker do first?" (closes eyes and counts to ten) "What do we shout after ten?" (ready or not, here I come) "Which spot hides you the best?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might giggle so loudly that finding them is a formality, choose the same perfect spot every single game, or hide WITH the seeker — the sweetest possible cheat.

Out in the real world

Hide and seek translates to every house you will ever visit — grandma’s, the hotel, the friend’s flat — and the rules your child knows travel with them.

Try it together

First games for threes: hide together — you and your child in one spot, giggling, while a grown-up seeks. Sardines round: one hider, everyone seeks, and every finder squeezes into the same hiding spot until only one seeker is left outside.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we count?" (out loud, to ten, eyes closed) "What is the rule about doors?" (no hiding where doors close)

This lesson pairs with the Hide and Seek flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hot Potato — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hot potato — the passing game played at comedy speed, where the loser’s punishment is three frog hops.

What is this?

Hot potato is a circle passing game: pass the potato hand to hand while the music plays — and whoever holds it when the music stops does one funny task.

What does it mean?

Fast, gentle passing is a real skill — the handover — practiced here at a speed that makes everyone laugh when it goes wrong.

What does the child need to know?

You need a soft potato-substitute (a ball, a beanbag, an actual potato) and music you can stop mid-song. Three or more players in a circle.

Why this matters

The music makes the passing hurry, and the hurry makes the game — but the losing is so gentle (three hops!) that nobody dreads the stop.

What it teaches

Quick handovers, left-to-right passing order, watching the object move around the ring, and losing with a laugh.

Words to learn

potatohotpassquickcirclestophop

Say this to your child

“"Pass it quick, pass it quick — the potato is hot! Do not hold it, do not drop it — pass, pass, pass! Music stopped... WHO has the potato? Hop like a frog!"”

Step by step

  1. Sit in a circle, knees almost touching.
  2. Start the music and pass the potato one way — say which way first: "pass it left!"
  3. Pass it quick — the potato is HOT, do not hold it!
  4. The DJ stops the music at a surprise moment.
  5. Whoever holds it does the funny task — hop three times, or quack like a duck — then the music starts again and the potato flies.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, many hands surround the potato from every direction — the hands reach in fast because the passing never stops while the music plays.

Ask your child

"Which way are we passing?" "What do we do if the music stops on us?" (the funny task — and we laugh) "Can we pass faster?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might hold the potato with two careful hands like it genuinely burns, speed-pass so hard the potato flies across the circle, or beg for the hop task on purpose.

Out in the real world

Any circle of kids with any ball can start this game in one chant — "hot potato!" — and now your child knows both the passing and the kind-losing script.

Try it together

Two-potato round: two potatoes start at opposite sides of the circle and cross in the middle. Reverse round: the DJ shouts "change direction!" mid-song and the passing flips.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do while the music plays?" (pass it quick) "What happens to the holder when it stops?" (one funny task, then we play again)

This lesson pairs with the Hot Potato flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Musical Chairs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches musical chairs — the furniture game where walking feet only, and the last chair is the championship.

What is this?

Musical chairs is a music game with chairs in a circle: walk while the music plays, sit when it stops — and one chair leaves the circle every round.

What does it mean?

The game is stopping-on-a-signal with a prize attached, and losing a chair kindly — then getting the DJ job — is the emotional lesson under the noise.

What does the child need to know?

You need one chair per player, minus one, and music. The living-room rule: walking feet only, never running, said out loud every round like a referee.

Why this matters

It is freeze dance with chairs — the same stop-on-the-signal skill, plus the wild joy of diving for a seat.

What it teaches

Walking control, listening for the stop, quick choosing, and the losing-then-helping loop.

Words to learn

chairscirclewalkmusicstopsitround

Say this to your child

“"Walk, walk, walk — walking feet! Here comes the music stopping... SIT! One chair goes away... walk again!"”

Step by step

  1. Put the chairs in a circle facing outward — one fewer chair than players.
  2. Say the rule: walking feet only. Say it again. Say it every round.
  3. Start the music — everyone walks around the outside of the chairs.
  4. Stop the music — everybody finds a chair and SITS.
  5. The player left standing becomes the DJ for the next round, and one chair leaves the circle. Last two players, last one chair — and a rematch for the crown.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a ring of chairs sits empty with music notes circling above — the chairs wait for the walking players, and the notes say the music could stop at any moment.

Ask your child

"What kind of feet do we use?" (walking feet) "What happens when the music stops?" (find a chair and sit) "What is the DJ’s job?" (stop the music — and start it again)

What your child can say or do

Your child might dive for chairs with full-commitment somersaults, lose round one with thundercloud eyebrows and win round five with a victory lap, or DJ with theatrical suspense.

Out in the real world

Every birthday party with more chairs than games ends up here — the child who knows the walking-feet rule and the DJ-job kindness is the one everyone wants back next time.

Try it together

Kind version for threes: two chairs for the final two players and a shared win, arms raised together. Strict version for fives: one chair, one champion, rematch on request.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many chairs are there?" (one fewer than players) "What do we do when the music stops?" (sit!) "What does the left-standing player get to be?" (the DJ)

This lesson pairs with the Musical Chairs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Red Light, Green Light — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches red light, green light — the racing game that practices the word STOP with whole bodies.

What is this?

Red light, green light is a racing game: the caller shouts green light (run!) and red light (freeze!) until one racer reaches the caller.

What does it mean?

Stopping on a word is a safety skill — the strongest "stop" a child owns is one their whole body has practiced.

What does the child need to know?

You need a stretch of hallway or yard and one caller. Any distance works: three meters is a full game, a whole yard is a championship.

Why this matters

The game is delicious because red light arrives WITHOUT warning — the racing feels too good to stop, and stopping anyway is the win.

What it teaches

Starting and stopping on a word, body control in sudden stillness, listening close enough to catch trick calls.

Words to learn

green lightred lightgostopfreezeracecaller

Say this to your child

“"Green light — GO! Red light — STOP like a statue! Green light... red light! Nobody move! ...Green light!"”

Step by step

  1. The caller stands at one end; the racers line up at the other.
  2. "Green light!" — everyone runs forward.
  3. "Red light!" — everyone freezes on the spot. Anyone still moving goes back to the start line (kindly, once).
  4. Green and red alternate — closer and closer to the caller.
  5. The first racer to reach the caller wins the round and becomes the new caller.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the child reaches toward a traffic light showing red and green — the two colors are the whole game, and the reaching arm shows the run that happens on green.

Ask your child

"What do we do on green?" (run forward) "What do we do on red?" (freeze on the spot) "What happens if we move on red?" (back to the start — kindly)

What your child can say or do

Your child might freeze mid-hop with one leg hanging in the air, invent a tip-toe shuffle to sneak on red, or call the lights with a caller voice borrowed from a traffic officer.

Out in the real world

Crossing streets, parking lots, sidewalks — the child whose body stops on the word red has practiced the most useful stop there is, and had a championship doing it.

Try it together

Trick round: the caller says "red light" in a green-light voice and "green light" in a whisper — catching players means watching the lights, not the lips. Slow-motion round: green means walk as slow as syrup.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which color means run?" (green) "Which color means stop?" (red) "What does the winner get to be?" (the caller)

This lesson pairs with the Red Light, Green Light flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bingo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches picture bingo — the table game with the loudest winning word in the world.

What is this?

Bingo is a matching game: the caller names pictures one by one, players cover the ones on their card, and a full row shouts BINGO.

What does it mean?

Bingo drills three skills at once — listening, matching and waiting for your turn to shout — with a winner moment big enough to remember.

What does the child need to know?

You need a bingo card per player (picture bingo for young players), something to cover squares with (beans, buttons, torn paper), and a caller.

Why this matters

The game moves at the caller’s speed, so it bends to the youngest player — and the shout at the end is pure delight.

What it teaches

Listening and holding the called picture in mind, scanning a grid for matches, taking turns, and the B-I-N-G-O letters riding along.

Words to learn

bingocardcallcovermatchrowshout

Say this to your child

“"Listen close — I call the picture, you find it and cover it. A star... a star! Who has a star? ...Every square in your row? Shout BINGO!"”

Step by step

  1. Every player takes a card and a little pile of covers.
  2. The caller picks a picture and says it clearly — twice: "a duck... a duck!"
  3. Find that picture on your card and cover it.
  4. Keep calling, one picture at a time — no racing, the caller sets the speed.
  5. A full row covered — across, up or down — earns the shout: BINGO! Then clear the cards and the new round begins.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the BINGO grid has checked squares, one star square and a letter-B ball beside it — the letters across the top are how real bingo cards name their rows.

Ask your child

"What do we do when the caller says a picture?" (find it and cover it) "When can we shout BINGO?" (when a whole row is covered) "Who wants to be the caller next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might cover squares they do not have and defend them fiercely, practice the shout alone in the other room, or call the pictures with a megaphone voice for their round as caller.

Out in the real world

Bingo nights happen at schools, churches, fairs and family reunions everywhere — a child who can play picture bingo can sit down at any of them.

Try it together

First games for threes: two-in-a-row wins, and the caller names each picture twice. Caller round: your child calls, you play — mishearing the caller is now their favorite joke.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the caller do?" (say the pictures, one at a time) "What do we cover our pictures with?" "What is the winning shout?" (BINGO!)

This lesson pairs with the Bingo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Fishing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fishing game — a paper pond, a magnet rod, and the steadiest hands in the house.

What is this?

The fishing game is a catching game: paper fish with paper-clip mouths swim on the floor, and a magnet-on-a-string rod lifts them out.

What does it mean?

The magnet does not hurry, so neither can the fisher — steady hands and patience are the whole catch.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper fish (cut simple fish shapes), one paper clip per fish, a stick, string and a small magnet. The floor is the pond.

Why this matters

Waiting for the clip to meet the magnet is a patience practice that ends in a genuine, satisfying CLICK — the best small win in quiet games.

What it teaches

Steady-hand control, patience and waiting, hand-eye targeting at a distance, and counting the catch.

Words to learn

fishrodlinehookcatchpondcount

Say this to your child

“"Hold the rod steady... let the line dangle... wait for it... wait for it... GOT ONE! You caught the pink fish! Into the bucket — now pass the rod on."”

Step by step

  1. Make the pond: scatter the paper fish on the floor, clips facing up.
  2. Make the rod: tie the string to the stick, tie the magnet to the string.
  3. Hold the rod with two hands and dangle the magnet over a fish.
  4. Hold VERY still — wait for the magnet and clip to find each other. CLICK!
  5. Lift the fish out and into your bucket, then pass the rod to the next fisher. Count the catch at the end.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the rod hooks one leaping fish while more fish swim in the little pond — the leaping one is the moment the clip meets the magnet.

Ask your child

"Why must we hold still?" (so the magnet can catch the clip) "How many fish did you catch?" "Which fish is the biggest?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might narrate every catch like a deep-sea captain, name all the fish, or hold the rod with tongue-out concentration that makes the waiting worth watching.

Out in the real world

Magnetic fishing rods come with every fishing-game set at every toy shop — and now your child can build the pond version from paper whenever the real one is out of reach.

Try it together

Two-rod round if waiting gets wobbly — one rod each, divided pond. Colors round: "catch only the pink fish!" Counting round: land exactly three fish, no more.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes the fish stick to the line?" (the magnet and the paper clip) "What do we do after our catch?" (lift it out, bucket it, pass the rod)

This lesson pairs with the Fishing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Four in a Row — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches four in a row — the dropping-discs game that is often a child’s very first strategy game.

What is this?

Four in a row is a grid game: take turns dropping discs into the columns, and the first player to line up four of their own wins.

What does it mean?

Planning is visible here — the grid shows every threat at once — so blocking, trapping and the double threat are all learnable at the table.

What does the child need to know?

You need the standing grid and two colors of discs — or a drawn grid and buttons, coins or two colors of cereal. Two players.

Why this matters

The rules take one minute to learn, the games take three minutes to play, and the losing teaches the next game — the perfect strategy starter.

What it teaches

Turn-taking, spotting patterns (rows and diagonals), blocking, and the long game of thinking one move ahead.

Words to learn

discdropcolumnrowslopeblockfour

Say this to your child

“"Drop your disc — clunk! Now I drop mine. You have three in a row? I block you! Watch the slopes — four can hide on an angle."”

Step by step

  1. Stand the grid up (or draw a 7-wide, 6-tall grid on paper).
  2. Take turns: choose a column and drop your disc in — it falls to the lowest empty space.
  3. Watch for your opponent’s three-in-a-row — that disc MUST be blocked.
  4. Build your own line: across, straight up, or on the diagonal slope.
  5. Four in a line wins the round — shout it, clear the grid, rematch.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the standing grid fills with pink and yellow discs and a few more wait beside it — the discs fall from the top, so every column builds from the bottom up.

Ask your child

"Where am I about to win? Block me!" "Where are YOU about to win?" "Can a win hide on a slope?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might develop the poker face, set up the sneaky double threat (two wins at once — nobody can block both), or lose round one and win round five with the exact block that beat them.

Out in the real world

The boxed game is sold everywhere as Connect Four — but a paper grid and two button colors play the identical game at restaurants, in waiting rooms, anywhere.

Try it together

Open-book games first: point out every threat out loud so blocking becomes the whole game. Then five silent rounds — strategies go secret, and the wins get earned.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many in a line wins?" (four) "Which directions can a line go?" (across, up, and the slope) "What do you do when I have three?" (block me)

This lesson pairs with the Four in a Row flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Memory Match — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches memory match — the flipping game known in the UK simply as pairs, where the remembering is the whole sport.

What is this?

Memory match is a card game: all cards face down, turn two on your turn — a matching pair is yours to keep, a miss goes back for someone to remember.

What does it mean?

The game trains the exact skill it is named for: holding a place AND a picture in mind across other people’s turns.

What does the child need to know?

You need a deck of matching pairs (picture cards, two of each) and a table. Start with three pairs — six cards — face down in a grid.

Why this matters

Young memories are mighty, and this is the game where a four-year-old honestly beats a grown-up — the fairness of it keeps everyone playing.

What it teaches

Visual memory (place plus picture), turn-taking, honest flipping (no peeking!), and the count of pairs won.

Words to learn

memorymatchpairturn overface downkeepagain

Say this to your child

“"Turn one card... now a second. Apple and apple — a PAIR! You keep them. Two different ones? Turn them back and remember where that apple lives..."”

Step by step

  1. Lay the pairs face down in a neat grid — six cards for the first game.
  2. On your turn, turn over exactly TWO cards, saying each out loud: "an apple... a duck."
  3. A pair! Keep them both — your turn continues with two more cards.
  4. A miss? Turn both back face down, in the same places — and remember where they were.
  5. When every pair is found, count the keeps. Most pairs wins — then shuffle and go again.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the grid holds face-down question-mark cards with two apple cards turned face up — the question marks are the memory part, and the apples are the find.

Ask your child

"Where was the other apple?" "How many pairs do you have?" "Should we make the grid bigger or keep it small?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might rest a helpful finger on the table where the match lives (gentle cheating — smile and allow it at first), gasp dramatically at every pair, or win six rounds straight and keep the score all week.

Out in the real world

In the UK the game is called pairs — a deck of cards and a kitchen table is all it takes, anywhere, any language: the pictures do the talking.

Try it together

Grow the grid as the finding gets fast: six cards, then twelve, then the whole deck. Grown-up handicap round: grown-up must say out loud where they THINK each missing card lives — narrating memory makes it stronger.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many cards do we turn on our turn?" (two) "What do we do with a pair?" (keep them) "What do we do with a miss?" (turn them back and remember)

This lesson pairs with the Memory Match flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Rock, Paper, Scissors — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches rock, paper, scissors — the two-second game that decides who goes first in every other game.

What is this?

Rock, paper, scissors is a hand game: both players make one of three shapes at the same moment, and the shapes decide the winner.

What does it mean?

The shapes beat each other in a circle — rock blunts scissors, scissors cut paper, paper wraps rock — so nothing is simply strongest, and every round is a fresh guess.

What does the child need to know?

You need two players and one free hand each. That is the entire equipment list — the most portable game ever invented.

Why this matters

Every game night needs a fair way to pick who goes first, and this one takes two seconds, needs nothing, and ends arguments before they start.

What it teaches

Fine-motor hand shapes on a signal, rhythm and timing in the chant, and losing fast without a fuss.

Words to learn

rockpaperscissorsfistpalmshootwinner

Say this to your child

“"Rock... paper... scissors... SHOOT! Show your hand! My rock breaks your scissors — I win this one! Again — best of three!"”

Step by step

  1. Make fists together and chant together: "rock... paper... scissors... SHOOT!"
  2. On SHOOT, both players show a hand shape: fist (rock), flat palm (paper), or two fingers (scissors).
  3. Compare: rock blunts scissors, scissors cut paper, paper covers rock.
  4. Same shape? A draw — chant again.
  5. Best of three crowns the round — then use the winner the way the playground does: they go first at whatever comes next.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three hands stand side by side — a fist for rock, an open palm for paper and two fingers for scissors — the three shapes every player chooses between.

Ask your child

"What beats rock?" (paper covers it) "What does a fist mean?" (rock) "What do we both say before the hands show?" (rock, paper, scissors, shoot!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might develop a lucky-rock strategy, chant faster and faster until hands blur, or referee every sibling dispute in the house for a week.

Out in the real world

Playgrounds, classrooms, back seats of cars on long drives — rock, paper, scissors settles disputes in every language, and the shapes never change.

Try it together

Tournament round: four players, winners play winners, champion crowned. New-shapes round (silly version): dynamite, water pistol, dragon — invent the rules together before playing, which is half the fun.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three shapes?" (rock, paper, scissors) "What beats scissors?" (rock) "When do the hands show?" (on SHOOT)

This lesson pairs with the Rock, Paper, Scissors flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tic-Tac-Toe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches tic-tac-toe — the first strategy game most children ever master, on a grid of nine squares.

What is this?

Tic-tac-toe is a grid game for two players: X and O take turns writing in the squares, and three of your mark in a row wins.

What does it mean?

The grid is small enough to see everything at once — so planning, blocking and the diagonal trick are all learnable on paper.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper and a pencil — or chalk on the sidewalk and two colors of stones. Two players; one draws X, one draws O.

Why this matters

The rules take ten seconds to teach, a game lasts under a minute, and the losing always shows you exactly what you missed — the perfect thinking game.

What it teaches

Turn-taking, grid scanning (rows, columns, diagonals), blocking, and the discovery that two careful players can always draw.

Words to learn

tic-tac-toegridXOrowcolumndiagonal

Say this to your child

“"You are X and I am O. Your X goes anywhere — now my O. Three in a row wins! Watch the diagonal — it is the sneaky one."”

Step by step

  1. Draw the grid: two lines across, two lines down — nine squares.
  2. Agree marks: one player is X, one is O.
  3. Take turns — X goes first this round, O first next round.
  4. Write your mark in any empty square. Three of yours in a line — across, down or diagonal — wins.
  5. Draw the winning line through your three, then wipe the grid and rematch — the loser goes first.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the three-by-three grid fills with pink X marks and purple O marks — every game starts as an empty nine-square grid and becomes a story of threes.

Ask your child

"Where are you about to win?" "Where am I about to win — and where must you block?" "Which square is the strongest first move?" (the middle, usually!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might develop the center-opening habit, win with a double threat nobody saw, or lose to a diagonal and spend the next hour studying diagonals.

Out in the real world

In the UK the same game is noughts and crosses — nought is the round O, cross is the X. It is played on paper, on sidewalks, on restaurant placemats, everywhere.

Try it together

Open-book games first: say every threat out loud ("if I go here, I win — block me!"). Then five silent rounds. Sidewalk round: chalk grid, stones and leaves for pieces.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many in a row wins?" (three) "Which three directions can a line go?" (across, down, diagonal) "What do we do to a three-in-a-row threat?" (block it)

This lesson pairs with the Tic-Tac-Toe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Maze — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches maze solving — the quiet game where the finger is the hero and every dead end is a clue.

What is this?

A maze is a path puzzle: travel from START to FINISH through the winding walls without crossing them.

What does it mean?

Solving a maze trains looking ahead, holding a plan, and calmly backing up from a dead end — resilience practice disguised as a puzzle.

What does the child need to know?

You need a maze (the card has one, and so does every activity book) and a finger — a pencil once the route is known.

Why this matters

Mazes are the quietest game on the shelf, and the win — reaching the FINISH star — is entirely the solver’s own.

What it teaches

Visual tracking, planning ahead one turn at a time, fine-motor tracing, and the patience of the wrong turn.

Words to learn

mazepathwalldead endtraceSTARTFINISH

Say this to your child

“"Finger on START... go slowly... this way... oops — a dead end! Back up, try the other path... there is the FINISH star! You solved it!"”

Step by step

  1. Find the START arrow and put a finger on it.
  2. Move slowly along the path — the finger is the traveler.
  3. Meet a fork? Look ahead at both paths — pick the one that goes further.
  4. Dead end? No problem — back the finger up and take the other path. Every dead end teaches the map.
  5. Reach the FINISH star — then trace the winning route again, fast, like a victory lap.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the maze has a START arrow, a FINISH star and one path already drawn through the purple walls — the drawn line is the route a brave finger took.

Ask your child

"Where does the path start?" "What do we do at a dead end?" (back up and try another path) "Can you find a shorter way than my finger took?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might solve it with two fingers racing each other, draw their own maze for you with three villainous dead ends, or refuse all help and solve it alone three times.

Out in the real world

Mazes wait in every activity book, every restaurant kids’ menu and every cereal box back — the finger-tracing practice is also the pencil-control practice school will ask for.

Try it together

Draw-your-own round: make a maze for someone else, with dead ends drawn on purpose — that is half the art. Timer round for fives: solve it before a slow count of thirty.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does every maze begin?" (at START) "What is a dead end?" (a path with no way through) "What do we do there?" (back up and try another way)

This lesson pairs with the Maze flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Puzzle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches puzzle solving — the quiet game where a broken picture becomes whole again, piece by piece.

What is this?

A puzzle is a picture cut into pieces: every piece has exactly one home, and solving means finding every home.

What does it mean?

Puzzles are shape-rotation practice — turning a piece in the mind until it fits — plus the patience to try, fail and try again.

What does the child need to know?

You need a jigsaw puzzle with big pieces (twelve pieces is a fine first size), a clear table, and the box picture facing up.

Why this matters

The last piece is the best feeling in quiet games, and everything before it is honest looking, turning and trying — no luck involved.

What it teaches

Shape matching, spatial rotation (flipping a piece in the mind), sorting by color and edge, and the stamina to finish.

Words to learn

puzzlepieceedgecornerfitturnlast piece

Say this to your child

“"Corners first! Find the flat-edge pieces — they make the border. Now the colors: all the sky pieces here. Does this one fit? Turn it... press... CLICK!"”

Step by step

  1. Look at the box picture first — say what you see: "a red barn, a big tree, a blue sky."
  2. Find the edge pieces — the ones with one flat side — and build the border.
  3. Sort the middle pieces into color piles: all the sky here, all the grass there.
  4. Try a piece: turn it, press gently — if it clicks, it belongs; if it will not fit, try turning it the other way.
  5. Fit the last piece — and count every piece in the finished picture together.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, four chunky jigsaw pieces wait in pink and purple, two already joined — the joining is the whole game, one click at a time.

Ask your child

"Which pieces have a flat side?" (the edges) "Where does this piece belong — near the sky or the grass?" "What happens if it does not fit?" (turn it, or try another piece)

What your child can say or do

Your child might insist on doing the border alone, cheat happily by checking the box every ten seconds (the box is legal!), or finish it, scramble it and start again immediately.

Out in the real world

Jigsaw puzzles live in every doctor’s waiting room and every grandparent’s shelf — the sorting and turning practice is the same geometry the classroom will ask for later.

Try it together

Twelve pieces is the first mountain; twenty-four is the graduation. Blind-sort round: name the color of each piece as you pick it up. Team round: you do the border, your child does the barn.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we build first?" (the border — the flat-edge pieces) "What do we do if a piece will not fit?" (turn it, try another way) "How does the last piece feel?" (the best!)

This lesson pairs with the Puzzle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Spot the Difference — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches spot the difference — the detective game where two nearly identical pictures hide a few sneaky changes.

What is this?

Spot the difference is a comparing game: two pictures sit side by side, and something — usually several things — is different.

What does it mean?

The eyes learn to sweep, hold and compare — the exact motion reading will ask for later — while the mouth practices saying what changed.

What does the child need to know?

You need a pair of near-twin pictures (the card has one; puzzle and activity books carry more) and sharp detective eyes.

Why this matters

Four-year-olds are magnificent at this game — grown-ups are reliably worse — so it is one of the few games your child may win on pure skill.

What it teaches

Visual comparison, systematic scanning (the sweep), describing changes out loud, and counting the finds.

Words to learn

samedifferentspotchangecomparefindextra

Say this to your child

“"Look at the two houses. Same, same, same... but WAIT — what is different? Look at the sky... look at the trees... count them!"”

Step by step

  1. Look at the left picture — really look: what is in it? A house, a tree, a cloud, a path.
  2. Now look at the right picture — same or different?
  3. Sweep slowly: sky first, then house, then garden, then path — one zone at a time.
  4. Found one? POINT and SAY it: "this picture has an extra cloud!"
  5. Count the changes together — how many did the two of you catch?

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the two house scenes are almost identical — one has an extra cloud in the sky and a missing tree by the path, and the differences hide in plain sight.

Ask your child

"How many changes did you find?" "Which one was the sneakiest?" "Look away — can you remember what the left picture had?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might circle every difference with a triumphant finger-slash, find one you missed and never let you forget it, or grab paper and draw their own tricky pair for you.

Out in the real world

Spot-the-difference puzzles wait in every kids’ menu, every magazine and every waiting room — the sweeping eyes are also the pre-reading eyes, practicing in disguise.

Try it together

Make-your-own round: draw a simple scene, copy it with one sneaky change, and challenge the family. Zones round: solve it zone by zone — "sky detectives first!"

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we look?" (slowly, one zone at a time) "What do we do when we find a change?" (point and say it out loud)

This lesson pairs with the Spot the Difference flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Treasure Hunt — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the treasure hunt — the game that turns your whole home into a map with an X on it.

What is this?

A treasure hunt is a clue game: each clue points to the next hiding spot, and the trail ends at the treasure.

What does it mean?

Following clues in order — read, go, look, read the next — is the skill behind every recipe, every school day and every map.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper for clues, a treasure (a snack, a sticker, a shiny stone), and five hiding spots that lead to each other in a chain.

Why this matters

The hunt has everything — mystery, running, reading-ish, and a golden ending — and it runs on nothing but paper and imagination.

What it teaches

Following directions in order, picture reading (clues for pre-readers), memory for places, and the delay-of-fun walk to the treasure.

Words to learn

treasurehuntcluehidefollowmapX

Say this to your child

“"Treasure hunt! Here is your first clue: go to the place where we keep the cold milk... the fridge! Look inside — another clue! Follow the trail, clue by clue, to the treasure!"”

Step by step

  1. Choose the treasure and its hiding place — the last stop on the trail.
  2. Work backwards: at each spot, leave the clue that leads to the NEXT spot.
  3. Write or draw the clues — pictures work for pre-readers: a drawing of the bookshelf means "go look on the bookshelf."
  4. Hand over clue one: "go to the place where we keep the cold milk... the fridge!"
  5. Follow the trail together — clue by clue — until the treasure is found, then swap: your child builds the next hunt for you.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the treasure map shows a dotted path from the palm tree past the X mark to a locked chest — the dotted line is the trail, and every clue is one step of it.

Ask your child

"Where does the clue send you?" "What was at the next spot?" "Which clue was the sneakiest?" "What was in the treasure?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might sprint each clue with a full adventure roar, build you a hunt in return (expect the treasure to be a sock), or hide the clues so well that the hunt becomes an archaeology dig.

Out in the real world

Hunts work at home, at grandma’s, at birthday parties and on rainy days — five clues and a cookie is a complete afternoon, and your child now knows how to build one from scratch.

Try it together

Picture-clue round for pre-readers: every clue is a drawing. Rhyme round for fives: "where your shoes line up in a row — go!" Builder round: your child hides everything and YOU hunt — being the seeker of a kid-built hunt is a delight.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does each clue tell you?" (where to go next) "Where does the trail end?" (at the treasure) "Who can build the next hunt?" (you — the hunter becomes the mapmaker)

This lesson pairs with the Treasure Hunt flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Charades — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches charades — the acting game where silence is the rule and guessing is the sport.

What is this?

Charades is a guessing game: one player acts something out without speaking, and everyone else shouts what it is.

What does it mean?

Acting without words is imagination plus body control — and guessing trains watching closely and thinking in possibilities.

What does the child need to know?

You need players and ideas: animals, actions, jobs. Write them on paper slips for the draw, or just whisper them ear to ear.

Why this matters

The silence rule makes everything funnier — a silent elephant, a wordless tooth-brush — and the guessing means every player is in the game every second.

What it teaches

Pretend play, body expression, reading other people’s acting, and the give-and-take of guessing kindly.

Words to learn

charadesactguesssilentanimalactionagain

Say this to your child

“"I will act like something and you guess what I am. No words from me — only moving! (hop, hop, hop) What am I? ...A bunny! Your turn — act like something BIG."”

Step by step

  1. Draw or whisper an idea — an animal first: "you are a bunny!"
  2. The actor moves without a word — hopping, nose-twitching, ears up.
  3. Everyone guesses out loud: "a kangaroo? a frog? A BUNNY!"
  4. The actor helps with signs: thumbs up for warmer, thumbs down for colder.
  5. A right guess ends the round with a cheer — and the guesser becomes the next actor.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one child acts out a move while two friends guess, with question marks floating over their heads — the question marks are the guessing, and the mid-air leg is the acting.

Ask your child

"What am I acting?" "What helped you guess?" "What will you act next — and can you do it without laughing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might act every animal in the zoo before the round ends, guess wildly and wonderfully wrong on purpose, or discover they can act "sleeping" so well that the room joins in.

Out in the real world

Charades fills family game nights, long rainy afternoons and restaurant waits — all it needs is imagination and a body, which every child already owns.

Try it together

Animals round first (the clearest moves), then actions round: brushing teeth, sleeping, kicking a ball. Timer round for fives: guess before a slow count of twenty.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the no-talking rule?" (the actor may not speak) "What does a thumbs-up mean?" (warmer — you are close) "Who acts next?" (the one who guessed right)

This lesson pairs with the Charades flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Simon Says — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches simon says — the listening game with a trap built into every round.

What is this?

Simon says is a listening game: obey every command that begins with "Simon says" — and freeze when the words are missing.

What does it mean?

The game trains catching exact words, holding an instruction in mind, and stopping an impulse — the whole attention toolkit, in a party game.

What does the child need to know?

You need two or more players and floor space to hop, spin and touch toes. The caller is called Simon — and Simon is allowed to be sneaky.

Why this matters

The trap is the joy: the command sounds exactly the same with or without "Simon says," and catching yourself mid-move is the funniest failure there is.

What it teaches

Careful listening for exact words, impulse stopping, following multi-step commands, and the caller’s skill of speaking clearly.

Words to learn

simon sayscommandlistenfreezetrickmagic words

Say this to your child

“"Simon says — touch your nose! Simon says — hop on one foot! Now... touch your toes! (did anybody move? no Simon says!) The magic words are SIMON SAYS."”

Step by step

  1. Everyone stands with room to move; the caller is Simon.
  2. "Simon says touch your nose!" — touch your nose. The magic words make it real.
  3. "Touch your toes!" — NO "Simon says"... do not move! Caught movers do one funny hop and rejoin.
  4. Mix honest commands with sneaky traps — the trap is the game.
  5. Swap the crown: the fastest listener becomes the next Simon, and the whole game starts again.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the child strikes a pose beside two cards showing a hand and a footprint — the cards are the commands, and only some of them carry the magic words.

Ask your child

"What are the magic words?" (Simon says) "What do we do when the words are missing?" (do not move!) "What does Simon have to do to be sneaky?" (say it just the same — no peeking hints)

What your child can say or do

Your child might freeze so hard at the first trap that they wobble, become a caller with theatrical slow-motion commands, or develop the poker face of a card shark.

Out in the real world

Classrooms play this game to practice listening; families play it because it is hilarious. The child who can catch the missing "Simon says" is practicing the same ear that follows teacher instructions.

Try it together

Speed round: commands come fast, one after another. Silly-command round: "Simon says walk like a robot" — obedience with style. Two-step round for fives: "Simon says touch your nose, THEN freeze" — both steps or you are caught.

Understanding check

Ask: "When do we obey?" (only when it starts with Simon says) "What happens when we move without the magic words?" (one funny hop, then we rejoin) "Who gets to be Simon next?" (the fastest listener)

This lesson pairs with the Simon Says flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hopscotch — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hopscotch — the chalk-and-sidewalk classic where the course is the math and the hopping is the sport.

What is this?

Hopscotch is a hopping game: throw a stone onto the numbered course, hop through the squares, and pick the stone up on the way back.

What does it mean?

Number order, balance and turn-taking all live on the ground — the sidewalk is the worksheet and the gym at once.

What does the child need to know?

You need chalk, a small stone (the marker), and a stretch of flat pavement. Two or more players; one is plenty for practice.

Why this matters

Every child can draw the course themselves — numbering the squares is the first job and the first math — and the game starts the moment the chalk stops.

What it teaches

One-foot balance, hopping power, number recognition and order, and the gentle discipline of taking turns.

Words to learn

hopscotchchalksquarenumberhopthrowturn

Say this to your child

“"Throw the stone — it landed on 4! Now hop: one foot, one foot, two feet, two feet... jump OVER square 4, turn at the top, and hop back to pick it up!"”

Step by step

  1. Draw the course with chalk: squares in a line — 1, then 2 and 3 side by side, then 4, then 5 and 6, up to 10.
  2. Say the numbers as you draw them — the course is the counting.
  3. Throw your stone onto a square — it must land flat inside the lines.
  4. Hop the course: one foot on single squares, two feet (one on each) on the pairs — and jump OVER the square with your stone.
  5. Turn at the top, hop back, and pick your stone up on the way. Then the next player throws.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the girl hops along the numbered chalk course from 1 to 10 — the side-by-side squares are where two feet land, one on each number.

Ask your child

"Which number did your stone land on?" "Which squares get two feet?" (the side-by-side pairs) "What do we do at the top of the course?" (turn and hop back)

What your child can say or do

Your child might redraw the course bigger every game, wobble magnificently on the one-foot squares, or develop a stone-throwing technique that always lands on the hardest number.

Out in the real world

Hopscotch is played on every continent under almost every name — chalk and pavement are all it takes, anywhere in the world.

Try it together

Two-foot round for beginners: hop the whole course on two feet, no stone yet. Counting round: say every number out loud as your foot lands. Championship: the wobbliest landing still standing wins.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we throw?" (the stone) "Where do two feet land?" (the side-by-side pairs) "When do we pick the stone up?" (on the way back)

This lesson pairs with the Hopscotch flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.

KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Jump Rope — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches jump rope — the swing-and-jump rhythm game the UK calls skipping, with the playground chants riding along.

What is this?

Jump rope is a rhythm game: swing the rope over your head, and hop over it as it sweeps the ground — one jump per swing.

What does it mean?

The rope teaches rhythm, timing and burst power — and the chants make the counting sing instead of work.

What does the child need to know?

You need a rope (any skipping rope) and a little clear space — indoors works if the ceiling is kind. One jumper, or two turners and one jumper.

Why this matters

The rope costs almost nothing, travels anywhere, and grows with the child — from first wobbly hops to double-dutch someday.

What it teaches

Rhythm and timing, burst-power jumping, wrist-turning coordination, and chanting-while-moving (two things at once!).

Words to learn

ropeswingjumpturnrhythmchantagain

Say this to your child

“"Swing it over — whoosh — and jump as it comes down! One jump! Again — two jumps! Two friends can turn the rope while you jump: jack be nimble, jack be quick..."”

Step by step

  1. First, no rope: jump in place to a count — one, two, three — knees soft.
  2. Take the rope: hold a handle in each hand, rope behind your heels.
  3. Swing it over your head — whoosh — and watch it come toward your feet.
  4. Jump! One small hop as the rope sweeps under — hands keep turning the whole time.
  5. Missed? That is a turn, not a failure — swing again. Count every jump that lands.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the girl jumps mid-air over her pink rope with motion marks under her shoes — the rope is mid-swing, and the small hop is exactly the size a real jump needs.

Ask your child

"When do we jump?" (as the rope sweeps down to our feet) "Who keeps the hands turning?" (the jumper — even mid-jump) "What chant shall we sing while we jump?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might master two jumps and demand a parade, chant playground rhymes at double speed while jumping, or practice so long the rope becomes the favorite toy of the summer.

Out in the real world

In the UK the same rope is a skipping rope and the game is skipping — same swing, same songs. Schoolyards, sidewalks and driveways all become arenas; the rope is the whole ticket.

Try it together

Helper round: a grown-up holds one handle and swings slowly while your child holds the other side and jumps — the shared swing teaches the timing. Chant round: every jump is one word of the rhyme.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do our hands do the whole time?" (keep turning the rope) "When do our feet jump?" (as the rope sweeps down) "What does the UK call this rope?" (a skipping rope)

This lesson pairs with the Jump Rope flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.
